title: How do you secure sensitive endpoints from brute-force attacks (rate limiting, account lockout, CAPTCHA, MFA, IP blacklisting, monitoring, short-lived tokens)?
shortTitle: How do you secure sensitive endpoints from brute-force attacks
topicTitle: How do you secure sensitive endpoints from brute-force attacks

s1_definition.profdef: Defending against brute-force attacks is a layered discipline because no single control is sufficient. Rate limiting caps how many attempts a client can make per time window; account lockout temporarily disables an account after too many failed logins; CAPTCHA forces a challenge that is hard to automate; multi-factor authentication requires a second proof so a guessed password alone is useless; IP blacklisting blocks known-abusive sources; monitoring and alerting detect attack patterns early; and short-lived tokens limit the value of any credential that is eventually guessed or stolen. Together they raise the cost of guessing credentials so high that the attack becomes impractical.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine thieves trying thousands of PINs at a National Bank of India ATM. Rate limiting is the machine only allowing a few tries per minute. Account lockout is the card being swallowed after three wrong PINs. CAPTCHA is the machine asking a question only a human can answer quickly. Multi-factor authentication is requiring both the card and a one-time code sent to Rajesh's phone, so a guessed PIN alone is worthless. IP blacklisting is banning a specific thief who keeps coming back. Monitoring is the security camera and the alarm that calls the guard when it sees a pattern of attacks. And short-lived tokens mean even a stolen access pass expires in minutes.
s1_definition.oneliner: Stop brute force with layers: rate-limit attempts, lock accounts after repeated failures, challenge with CAPTCHA, require MFA so a password alone is useless, blacklist abusive IPs, monitor and alert on patterns, and keep tokens short-lived.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Defending against brute-force attacks is a layered discipline because no single control is sufficient. Rate limiting caps how many attempts a client can make per time window; account lockout temporarily disables an account after too many failed logins; CAPTCHA forces a challenge that is hard to automate; multi-factor authentication requires a second proof so a guessed password alone is useless; IP blacklisting blocks known-abusive sources; monitoring and alerting detect attack patterns early; and short-lived tokens limit the value of any credential that is eventually guessed or stolen. Together they raise the cost of guessing credentials so high that the attack becomes impractical.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine thieves trying thousands of PINs at a National Bank of India ATM. Rate limiting is the machine only allowing a few tries per minute. Account lockout is the card being swallowed after three wrong PINs. CAPTCHA is the machine asking a question only a human can answer quickly. Multi-factor authentication is requiring both the card and a one-time code sent to Rajesh's phone, so a guessed PIN alone is worthless. IP blacklisting is banning a specific thief who keeps coming back. Monitoring is the security camera and the alarm that calls the guard when it sees a pattern of attacks. And short-lived tokens mean even a stolen access pass expires in minutes.

**One line to remember:** Stop brute force with layers: rate-limit attempts, lock accounts after repeated failures, challenge with CAPTCHA, require MFA so a password alone is useless, blacklist abusive IPs, monitor and alert on patterns, and keep tokens short-lived.

sections.s2_technical:
Brute force means an attacker systematically tries many credential combinations, either guessing one account's password through many tries, or credential stuffing with leaked username and password pairs across many accounts. The defence is defence in depth, because each control covers a gap another leaves open, and an attacker must defeat all of them at once.

Rate limiting is the first line. You cap the number of requests a client may make in a window, for example five login attempts per minute per account and per IP, and reject excess attempts with a 429 Too Many Requests. Implementations use a counter in a fast store like Redis with a sliding or fixed window, or token-bucket and leaky-bucket algorithms. Rate limiting is applied best at the API gateway so it protects every service uniformly, and you rate-limit by multiple keys, such as account, IP, and device, so an attacker cannot simply spread attempts.

Account lockout temporarily disables an account after a threshold of consecutive failed logins, for example locking for fifteen minutes after five failures. This directly stops single-account guessing. The nuance is that naive lockout enables a denial-of-service, where an attacker intentionally fails logins to lock out a legitimate user, so you prefer progressive delays, lock by IP plus account rather than account alone, and notify the real user, rather than hard permanent locks.

CAPTCHA inserts a challenge that is cheap for a human but expensive for a bot, shown after a few failed attempts rather than on every login so legitimate users are not annoyed. It blunts automated scripts specifically. It is not foolproof because solving services exist, so it is one layer, not the whole defence.

Multi-factor authentication is the strongest single control because it breaks the economics of guessing a password. Even if the attacker guesses the password, they still need a second factor, like a one-time code from an authenticator app, an SMS code, or a hardware key. For sensitive banking actions you require MFA on login and often step-up MFA on high-risk operations like a large transfer, so the password alone is never enough.

IP blacklisting blocks sources that show abusive behaviour, either statically from threat intelligence or dynamically when a source trips your rate limits or failure thresholds. It is effective against a persistent single source but weak against distributed attacks from many IPs or botnets, so it complements rather than replaces the other layers, and you combine it with reputation scoring and geo rules.

Monitoring and alerting turn silent attacks into visible ones. You log authentication outcomes, track metrics like failed-login rate and lockout counts, and alert when they spike, so an on-call engineer or an automated response can react. Detecting a surge of failures across many accounts reveals credential stuffing that per-account lockout alone would miss.

Short-lived tokens limit the damage once something is compromised. Access tokens expire in minutes and are paired with refresh tokens, so a stolen or eventually-guessed credential has a tiny window of usefulness, and refresh-token rotation detects reuse. This does not prevent guessing but reduces its payoff.

Senior nuances: always hash passwords with a slow algorithm like BCrypt or Argon2 so even an offline guess is expensive; return a generic failure message so you do not reveal whether the username or the password was wrong; apply the same throttling to password-reset and one-time-code endpoints, which are common blind spots; and combine signals, treating many weak signals like unusual geography, new device, and rising failure rate as a risk score that triggers step-up authentication.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India saw thousands of rapid login attempts against Rajesh's account from one source trying to guess his password. This is exactly rate limiting plus IP handling, capping attempts per account and per IP and rejecting the flood.

Problem 2 — After the flood continued, the account needed temporary protection so guessing could not continue indefinitely. This is exactly account lockout, disabling logins for a cooldown after repeated failures, done carefully to avoid locking out the real user permanently.

Problem 3 — Even if a password were guessed, the bank must ensure it is not enough. This is exactly multi-factor authentication, requiring a one-time code so the password alone fails.

Our mini-project demonstrates the layered defence. The code defines a `RateLimiter` with a per-key sliding window, a `LoginThrottle` that tracks failures and triggers lockout and CAPTCHA, an `MfaVerifier`, an `IpBlacklist`, and an `AuthService` that composes them, with a demo that shows a brute-force burst being rate-limited, an account being locked after repeated failures, CAPTCHA being demanded, and a correct password still failing without MFA.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: an attacker repeatedly submitting wrong passwords for Rajesh's account from one IP, then a legitimate login attempt.

Step 1: Each attempt first checks the IP blacklist, then the rate limiter keyed by account and IP. The first few attempts pass the rate limit but fail on the wrong password, and each failure is recorded by the throttle and logged for monitoring.

Step 2: After three failures the throttle now requires a CAPTCHA, so further attempts without a solved challenge are rejected with a CAPTCHA-required message, which specifically stops automated scripts.

Step 3: The rapid burst exceeds the rate limit, so the limiter rejects with a 429 and the service dynamically blacklists the abusive IP, stopping that source entirely. Meanwhile, after five failures the account is locked for a cooldown so guessing cannot continue even from a fresh IP.

Step 4: A legitimate user then supplies the correct password but no MFA code. The service accepts the password but rejects the login because the second factor is missing, proving that a guessed or correct password alone is never enough.

Step 5: Finally the legitimate user supplies the correct password, a solved CAPTCHA, and a valid MFA code, so the service clears the failure count and issues a short-lived token that expires in minutes, limiting the value of any future theft. The output shows the blocked attempts, the lockout, the CAPTCHA demand, the MFA rejection, and the final success.

```
2026-10-24 15:02:50 WARNING attempt 4 blocked: CAPTCHA required
2026-10-24 15:02:50 WARNING attempt 6 blocked: 429 rate limit exceeded
2026-10-24 15:02:50 WARNING attempt 7 blocked: IP blacklisted
2026-10-24 15:02:50 SEVERE  correct password alone rejected: account temporarily locked
2026-10-24 15:02:50 INFO    login SUCCESS for SAV2001 → issue short-lived token (5 min)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Login attempt (account, password, ip, captcha?, mfaCode?)
    │
    ▼

    │ no
    ▼
  Rate limiter (account+ip, 5/min) ──over──▶ 429 + blacklist the IP
    │ ok
    ▼
  Account locked? ──yes──▶ REJECT (15-min cooldown)
    │ no
    ▼
  ≥3 failures & no CAPTCHA? ──yes──▶ REJECT (CAPTCHA required)
    │ no / solved
    ▼
  Password correct? ──no──▶ record failure (→ lock at 5) ─▶ generic "invalid credentials"
    │ yes                     (monitoring: failed-login metric)
    ▼
  MFA valid? ──no──▶ REJECT (second factor required)
    │ yes
    ▼
  SUCCESS → issue SHORT-LIVED token (5 min) + reset failure count
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Layered Brute-Force Controls (FAANG Level) ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Chain of Responsibility: each guard checked in order          │
  │   WHY: a request must pass every layer; any layer can reject   │
  │ Token Bucket / Sliding Window: rate limiting                  │
  │   WHY: cap attempt rate per key fairly                        │
  │ Strategy: MFA factor (TOTP / SMS / hardware)                  │
  │   WHY: swap second-factor method without touching auth flow   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ───────────────────────────────────┐
  │ S: RateLimiter limits; LoginThrottle locks; MfaVerifier verifies│
  │ O: new control = new guard, AuthService composes them          │
  │ L: any MFA strategy substitutes another                        │
  │ D: AuthService depends on each guard's abstraction             │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ─────────────────────────────────────────────
  ┌──────────────┐ composes ┌──────────────┐
  │ AuthService   │─────────▶│ RateLimiter   │
  │ +login()      │─────────▶│ LoginThrottle │
  │               │─────────▶│ MfaVerifier   │
  │               │─────────▶│ IpBlacklist   │
  └──────────────┘          └──────────────┘

  ── Account State (lockout) ────────────────────────────────────
  [OPEN] ──fail×3──▶ [CAPTCHA_REQUIRED] ──fail×5──▶ [LOCKED 15m]
     ▲                                                  │
     └────────── success / cooldown elapsed ────────────┘

  ── Call Chain ────────────────────────────────────────────────
  1. blacklist.isBlocked(ip)?        → reject
  2. rateLimiter.allow(account+ip)?  → 429 + blacklist
  3. throttle.isLocked(account)?      → reject
  4. throttle.captchaRequired()?      → demand CAPTCHA
  5. password correct? → else record failure (generic msg)
  6. mfa.verify(code)? → else reject
  7. success → short-lived token + reset
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Defending sensitive endpoints from brute force is a layered discipline, because no single control is enough and an attacker must defeat all of them at once. Brute force means systematically trying many credential combinations, either guessing one account's password or credential-stuffing leaked pairs across many accounts, so I apply defence in depth where each control covers a gap the others leave open.

Rate limiting is the first line: I cap attempts per time window, for example five logins per minute keyed by both account and IP, and reject excess with a 429, usually enforced at the gateway with Redis counters or a token-bucket algorithm, and I key by multiple dimensions so an attacker cannot just spread the load. Account lockout temporarily disables an account after repeated failures, which stops single-account guessing, but I apply it carefully with progressive delays and locking by IP plus account rather than account alone, because naive lockout lets an attacker deny service to the real user. CAPTCHA adds a challenge that is cheap for a human but expensive for a bot, shown only after a few failures so legitimate users are not annoyed, and it specifically blunts automated scripts.

Multi-factor authentication is the strongest single control because it breaks the economics of guessing: even a correct password is useless without the second factor, like a one-time code or a hardware key, and for high-risk actions like a large transfer I require step-up MFA. IP blacklisting blocks sources that show abusive behaviour, statically from threat intelligence or dynamically when a source trips my limits, though it is weak against distributed botnets so it complements rather than replaces the other layers. Monitoring and alerting turn silent attacks into visible ones by tracking failed-login rates and lockout counts and paging when they spike, which catches credential stuffing across many accounts that per-account lockout alone would miss. And short-lived tokens limit the damage after any compromise, because an access token that expires in minutes with refresh rotation gives a stolen credential a tiny window of use.

On my project at National Bank of India we faced exactly this when thousands of rapid attempts hit Rajesh's account from one source, so the gateway rate-limited and then dynamically blacklisted the IP, the account locked after repeated failures, a CAPTCHA was demanded after three, and even a correct password failed without the MFA code. The nuances I always add are to hash passwords with a slow algorithm like BCrypt or Argon2 so even an offline guess is costly, to return a generic failure message so I never reveal whether the username or the password was wrong, to apply the same throttling to password-reset and one-time-code endpoints which are common blind spots, and to combine weak signals like unusual geography, a new device, and a rising failure rate into a risk score that triggers step-up authentication.

The one-line summary I give an interviewer is that I stop brute force with layers: rate-limit attempts per account and IP, lock accounts after repeated failures without enabling denial of service, challenge with CAPTCHA, require MFA so a password alone is useless, blacklist abusive IPs, monitor and alert on failure spikes, and keep tokens short-lived so any eventual compromise has a tiny blast radius.
